newsitem.title: USA: Hashimoto-Clinton summit focuses on trade, surplus.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto-Clinton summit focuses on trade, surplus.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's meeting with President Bill Clinton deepened bilateral relations but raised troublesome trade and economic issues that Hashimoto had hoped to avoid.

During a three-hour meeting, the two leaders agreed that Japan will promote strong domestic demand-led growth and avoid a significant increase in Tokyo's trade surplus, a senior Japanese government official said.

Hashimoto and Clinton did not discuss how Japan would achieve those goals despite signs the Japanese economy will continue to make only moderate growth and that Tokyo's trade surplus is set for a series of sharp rises, a Japanese spokesman said.

Clinton told Hashimoto at the meeting that he had instructed U.S. trade negotiators to seek progress in bilateral trade negotiations over specific trade items such as telecommunications, civil airline service and market access.
Before the summit, Japan was hopeful that Clinton would not bring up specific trade issues.
Japan's trade surplus with the United States has been rising over the past six months from year-earlier levels. It rose 11.2 percent in March to $3.04 billion.

Washington has repeatedly called on Japan not to depend on stepped-up exports to fuel faster growth and instead to enliven domestic demand so as to absorb more imports. The United States had expressed fears the April 1 increase in Japan's sales tax would dampen consumption.

Clinton expressed concern that Japan's tight fiscal policy entails risks of slowing economic growth, pushing up its external surplus and thus stimulating trade protectionist moves in the United States.
"I think the United States deepened its understanding of our fiscal condition and trade situations," a senior Japanese government official told Reuters.
Japan explained its surplus in goods and services trades accounts for only 0.5 percent to the nation's gross domestic products, one of the smallest among major industrial nations.
What Japan can do now to stimulate its economy is limited as Hashimoto has said he is committed to sticking to fiscal tightening due to a huge budget deficit.
A cut in interest rates -- one of the traditional methods to stimulate the economy along with an injection of public money -- is considered unlikely by analysts.
Hashimoto said deregulation of the Japanese economy and reforms of Japan's traditional financial, administrative, and fiscal systems will eventually help prop up the economy.
On the deregulation front, Japan and the U.S. agreed to intensify bilateral talks on Japan's deregulation.
U.S. officials said they want to ensure that Japan's deregulation efforts will indeed help open its markets to more foreign-made goods.
